bills.title: Gateway Partnership Act
bills.official_title: To authorize the Secretary of the Interior to enter into an agreement with the Gateway Arch Park Foundation to host private events in Gateway Arch National Park buildings, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by a Democrat with 2 cosponsors, the bill cleared the House by voice vote under suspension of the rules — a path used for measures with broad, bipartisan agreement — and the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee ordered it reported without amendment. Its narrow scope, a one-time partnership at a single national park, draws little organized opposition, so the main obstacle is competition for limited Senate floor time rather than substantive resistance.
bills.summary: This bill lets the National Park Service sign a one-time agreement with the Gateway Arch Park Foundation to hold private events at Gateway Arch National Park, including inside Park buildings like the Arch Visitor Center and the Old Courthouse. The agreement can last up to five years, must include terms protecting the Park, and must charge fees that cover the government's costs.
bills.brief: Authorizes a one-time National Park Service agreement letting the Gateway Arch Park Foundation host private, paid events in Gateway Arch National Park buildings, for a term of no more than five years.

top_lines.headline: Private Events at Gateway Arch
subs: One-time National Park Service agreement with the Gateway Arch Park Foundation
Agreement term capped at five years
Covers the Arch Visitor Center, Old Courthouse, and other public Park buildings

top_lines.headline: Cost Recovery and Safeguards
subs: Secretary must charge fees for event wear-and-tear
Government may recover all event costs, including security and personnel
Foundation must carry liability insurance naming the United States

top_lines.headline: Limits and Sunset
subs: Authority sunsets 7 years after enactment
Events cannot disrupt public access to the Park
Report to Congress due within 4 years

sections.label: Section 3 — Gateway Arch National Park Partner Agreement Pilot Project

items.main: Authorizes a one-time agreement, for a period not to exceed five years, letting the Gateway Arch Park Foundation host private events at the Park, which may include the use of Park buildings.
items.detail: The Secretary of the Interior may enter the agreement, which must include terms protecting the Park's resources — exclusive-use dates and times, a maximum number of events per month, National Park Service staffing levels, and liability insurance listing the United States as additionally insured. Events must be consistent with the Park's purposes and may not disrupt public use or access.

items.main: Requires the Secretary to charge a fee covering event wear-and-tear and allows recovery of all costs incurred from the private events.
items.detail: Recoverable costs include maintenance, utilities, administrative expenses, security, and personnel. Nothing in the Act prevents the National Park Service from hosting its own events or issuing permits to other parties.

items.main: Sunsets the agreement authority 7 years after enactment and requires a report to Congress within 4 years.
items.detail: Any existing agreement also terminates at the seven-year mark. The report to the House Committee on Natural Resources and the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources must cover operational impacts on visitor access, security, staffing, and facilities, and financial results including fees collected and costs recovered.

underreported.summary: The required agreement terms must include a provision stating the Federal Government will not be held liable for injuries or deaths from any cause resulting from the Foundation's occupancy and use of specified Park buildings.
underreported.why_unreported: The section reads as a partnership and events authorization, but this term shifts injury-and-death liability during private events away from the United States regardless of cause.

gaps: The bill requires the agreement to set a maximum number of events per month but does not set that cap itself.
The bill limits the agreement to the Gateway Arch Park Foundation but does not address the agreement if the Foundation stops serving as the Park's philanthropic partner.
The bill requires the Secretary to recover costs and report on fees collected but does not direct where recovered funds are deposited or how they may be spent.

added: A one-time National Park Service authority to enter a private-events agreement with the Gateway Arch Park Foundation, sunsetting 7 years after enactment.
Authority for the Secretary to charge fees and recover all costs from the private events.

bills.title: Geothermal Energy Advancement Act
bills.official_title: To promote responsible geothermal energy development on public lands, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: A Republican-sponsored permitting bill with 5 cosponsors, it passed the House by voice vote under suspension of the rules and was ordered reported without amendment by the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee — signals of bipartisan backing, as geothermal development draws support across party lines. Environmental groups may object to the categorical-exclusion expansion in Section 8, but that has not slowed the bill so far; the chief remaining hurdle is Senate floor scheduling.
bills.summary: This bill speeds up and adds new rules for geothermal energy projects on federal public land. It sets a 60-day deadline for the Interior Department to decide certain geothermal authorizations after reviews are done, lets the government charge developers for permitting costs through 2033, creates a Geothermal Ombudsman and permitting task force, and updates geothermal royalty and environmental-review rules.
bills.brief: Amends the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970 to accelerate federal geothermal permitting, adding decision deadlines, cost recovery, a Geothermal Ombudsman, and updated royalty and environmental-review rules.

top_lines.headline: Faster Geothermal Permitting
subs: 60-day decision deadline once federal reviews are complete
Deadline holds even with a pending lawsuit, unless a court blocks it
Interior may charge developers for permitting and inspection costs
Cost recovery runs through September 30, 2033

top_lines.headline: Geothermal Ombudsman and Task Force
subs: New Bureau of Land Management Geothermal Ombudsman within 60 days
Permitting task force can assign staff across BLM offices
Retention allowances capped at 25% of basic pay

top_lines.headline: Royalty, NEPA, and Standards Updates
subs: Reduced-royalty 10-year window tied to a facility's in-service date
Adds geothermal to NEPA categorical-exclusion streamlining
'Gold Book' operating standards updated and renamed for geothermal

sections.label: Section 2 — Permit Processing During Pending Litigation

items.main: Requires Interior to approve, issue, or deny a geothermal authorization within 60 days after completing all required federal reviews, even if a related civil action is pending.
items.detail: The deadline covers geothermal drilling permits, sundry notices, notices to proceed, rights-of-way, and other authorizations under a valid existing lease, unless a federal court vacates or grants injunctive relief for the lease or authorization. Required reviews include the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969, the Endangered Species Act of 1973, and division A of subtitle III of title 54. The bill states it grants no new authority to federal courts.

items.main: Lets Interior require geothermal lease applicants and holders to reimburse the United States for reasonable permitting and inspection costs, from enactment through September 30, 2033.
items.detail: Recoverable costs cover processing applications — operations plans, drilling permits, utilization plans, site licenses, and construction and commercial-use permits — and inspecting or monitoring exploration, drilling, and well-site work. The Secretary must consider any existing cost-share agreement and may reduce reimbursement for economic hardship or to promote greater use of geothermal resources. Reimbursements are credited as discretionary offsetting collections, available only as provided in advance in appropriations Acts.

sections.label: Section 6 — Geothermal Ombudsman and Task Force

items.main: Creates a Bureau of Land Management Geothermal Ombudsman and a Geothermal Permitting Task Force within 60 days of enactment.
items.detail: The Ombudsman acts as a liaison across BLM field, district, and State offices, provides dispute resolution for permit applicants, monitors permit timelines, and coordinates with the Federal Permitting Improvement Steering Council. The task force may assign personnel across offices, who must work in person, and may pay retention allowances of up to 25% of basic pay, subject to appropriations.

items.main: Section 5 directs Interior to update and rename the Bureau of Land Management's 'Gold Book' operating standards for geothermal.
items.detail: Interior must identify geothermal leasing and permitting standards within one year, publish an updated Gold Book within 270 days of doing so, and rename it to reflect geothermal development. The Gold Book is BLM's 'Surface Operating Standards and Guidelines for Oil and Gas Exploration and Development' (fourth edition, last revised 2007), and must be reviewed at least every five years.

sections.label: Section 7 — Geothermal Royalties and NEPA Review

items.main: Changes how the reduced-royalty period for geothermal electricity is measured and defines the facility it applies to.
items.detail: Royalties are computed with respect to a geothermal electric generating facility, and the reduced-royalty window shifts from the first 10 years of production under the lease to each year of the 10-year period following the facility's in-service date. The bill adds definitions of 'geothermal electric generating facility' and 'in-service date' to the Geothermal Steam Act.

items.main: Section 8 adds geothermal to a NEPA streamlining provision of the Energy Policy Act of 2005.
items.detail: Section 390 of the Energy Policy Act of 2005 is amended so geothermal exploration and development under the Geothermal Steam Act qualify for the same categorical-exclusion treatment previously limited to oil and gas.

underreported.summary: Extends the oil-and-gas categorical exclusion under Section 390 of the Energy Policy Act of 2005 to geothermal exploration and development.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's stated focus is permitting efficiency and oversight, but this provision changes the level of environmental review geothermal projects receive by adding them to an existing oil-and-gas streamlining category.

gaps: The bill sets a 60-day deadline to decide authorizations after reviews are complete but sets no deadline for completing those underlying reviews.
The bill authorizes cost recovery from developers but does not set fee amounts or a rate schedule, leaving them to the Secretary.
The bill creates an Ombudsman to resolve permitting disputes but gives applicants no appeal or enforcement mechanism if the 60-day deadline is missed.
The bill ends cost-recovery authority on September 30, 2033 but does not address how permitting costs are funded after that date.

added: A 60-day decision deadline for certain geothermal authorizations after federal reviews are complete.
A Geothermal Ombudsman and Geothermal Permitting Task Force within the Bureau of Land Management.
Interior cost-recovery authority for geothermal permitting and inspection, through September 30, 2033.
modified: Geothermal royalty timing under the Geothermal Steam Act — the reduced-royalty 10-year window is measured from a facility's in-service date rather than the first 10 years of production under the lease.
Section 390 of the Energy Policy Act of 2005 — categorical NEPA exclusions extended from oil and gas to also cover geothermal.
The Bureau of Land Management's 'Gold Book' operating standards — updated for geothermal and renamed.

bills.title: Wintergreen Emergency Egress Act
bills.official_title: To require the Secretary of the Interior to issue a right-of-way for an emergency exit on certain National Park Service land in the State of Virginia, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by a Republican with 7 cosponsors, this narrow, local measure — a single emergency-exit right-of-way for one Virginia community — passed the House by voice vote under suspension of the rules and was ordered reported without amendment by the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. Its limited scope and public-safety rationale attract little opposition, so enactment depends mainly on Senate floor time, often secured by attachment to a larger public-lands package.
bills.summary: This bill requires the Interior Department to grant a right-of-way through the Blue Ridge Parkway for an emergency exit serving the Wintergreen area in Virginia. Interior must first report to Congress that it has evaluated alternatives, analyzed fire risk, and completed the required environmental reviews.
bills.brief: Requires the Secretary of the Interior to issue a right-of-way across the Blue Ridge Parkway for an emergency exit at Wintergreen, Virginia, after completing specified studies and reviews.

top_lines.headline: Mandatory Emergency-Exit Right-of-Way
subs: Interior must grant a right-of-way through the Blue Ridge Parkway
For an emergency exit near Milepost 9.6 at Wintergreen, Virginia
Changes existing 'may issue' authority to 'shall issue'

top_lines.headline: Conditions Before Issuance
subs: Interior must first evaluate alternatives that avoid Federal land
Requires a fire-ecology analysis for a fire emergency
Requires completion of NEPA and title 54 reviews

sections.label: Section 2 — Right-of-Way for Emergency Exit, Blue Ridge Parkway

items.main: Amends the Act of June 30, 1936 to require, rather than authorize, the Secretary of the Interior to issue a right-of-way for a designated emergency exit near Milepost 9.6.
items.detail: The right-of-way follows the 'Proposed Egress' on the Interior map entitled 'Blue Ridge Parkway, Proposed Wintergreen Emergency Egress Near Milepost 9.6', numbered 601/194,694 and dated September 2024. Issuance becomes mandatory only after the Secretary reports to the House Committee on Natural Resources and the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

items.main: Requires three findings to be reported before the right-of-way is issued.
items.detail: The Secretary must report that an evaluation of egress alternatives that do not cross Federal land — including whether existing trails can be converted to roads — is complete; that an analysis of expected fire ecology behavior in a fire emergency is complete; and that required reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 and division A of subtitle III of title 54 are complete.

underreported.summary: Once the Secretary reports the three findings complete, issuing the right-of-way becomes mandatory ('shall issue') rather than discretionary.
underreported.why_unreported: The section is captioned as authorizing a right-of-way, but the operative change removes the Secretary's discretion to decline it after the required studies are reported complete.

gaps: The bill requires an evaluation of alternatives that do not cross Federal land but does not require the Secretary to adopt an alternative if a feasible one is found.
The bill requires a fire-ecology analysis but does not state what findings, if any, would prevent issuance of the right-of-way.
The bill makes issuance mandatory once the reports are complete but sets no deadline for completing those reports and reviews.

added: A mandatory duty for the Secretary of the Interior to issue the specified Blue Ridge Parkway right-of-way for the Wintergreen emergency exit, once the required findings are reported.
modified: Section 2 of the Act of June 30, 1936 (16 U.S.C. 460a-3) — the Secretary's authority to issue this right-of-way changes from discretionary ('may issue') to mandatory ('shall issue'), subject to conditions.
